<meta>continues from previous page</meta>thence its powers, namely for expelling, may be rendered stronger, and furthermore the doses of precipitated Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij præcipitati"</note> may be more easily formed into the shape of pills for administration or swallowing. This precipitated Mercury is therefore uniquely praised and commended, and truly it performs very well. The Mercury of Life <term>Mercurius vitæ</term> <gloss>antimony oxychloride, a potent emetic and purgative</gloss> or flowers of butter of antimony <note>original: "flores butyri antimonij"</note>, concerning which we spoke above, achieves the same effect if 4 to 12 grains of it are administered for three full days in an extract of Hellebore and Bitter Apple <term>colocynthidis</term>; it most successfully expels the resolved salt <note>the dissolved metallic salts or bodily fluids thought to cause the disease</note>. 

Afterward, however, sweating and urination should be provoked with a decoction of sarsaparilla, holy wood <note>guaiacum</note>, or asarum root, always adding spirit of Tartar or other diaphoretics <gloss>sweat-inducing agents</gloss> and diuretics, as mentioned above. This is best done by adding the secret remedy <term>arcanum</term> of wormwood or blessed thistle. Here it must be noted, however, that the three-day administration of Mercury of Life often tends to produce a prolapse of the anus <note>original: "procidētiā ani"</note> in adults, which is afterwards rarely or even with difficulty cured. 

In curing dropsy <term>hydrops</term> <gloss>edema or fluid retention</gloss>, it is necessary that such purgatives be applied immediately from the beginning of the cure; afterward, diuretics and hydrotics <note>medicines to remove water</note> should follow. Otherwise, the order would be backwards <term>ὕστερον πρότερον</term> <gloss>the latter put before the former</gloss>; all the serum or water would be rolled down to the kidneys and ureters, where afterwards, because of the heavy burden, very persistent symptoms often arise. 

Furthermore, in the preparation of the extract of black Hellebore root, it is safer to use wine itself instead of spirit of wine <note>alcohol</note>, in which the root should only be gently simmered without a loud boiling noise; this must be done with fresh wine until all the essential power has been extracted from the roots. Afterward, the extract should be reduced by evaporation or distillation to the thickness of honey. Spirit of wine, because of its power, is characterized by sulfur <note>alchemical sulfur, the flammable or oily principle</note> rather than being a simple liquor.

<sig>Y 3</sig>

<summary>Crollius describes the use of precipitated mercury and antimony for treating dropsy, emphasizing the correct order of treatment—purgation followed by diuretics—to avoid kidney damage. He provides specific instructions for extracting black Hellebore using wine rather than strong spirits.</summary>

<keywords>precipitated mercury, Mercury of Life, antimony, Hellebore, Bitter Apple, colocynthis, dropsy, hydrops, sarsaparilla, spirit of Tartar, diuretics, pharmaceutical preparation</keywords>
